content: The New York Academy of Sciences is recognized as the third-oldest scientific society in the United States. It operates as an independent, non-profit organization with a membership exceeding 25,000 individuals from 140 countries. The Academy's mission is to advance the understanding of science and technology. It actively identifies and promotes scientific advancements across various disciplines, transcending professional and geographic boundaries. Additionally, it fosters collaboration and synergy between institutions and individuals. The Academy contributes to the expansion of scientific knowledge by organizing meetings, seminars, and interdisciplinary conferences that bring together leading experts. It also disseminates information through both print and electronic media. The current president of the Academy is John Sexton, who also serves as the president of New York University. The Academy's programs are diverse and include its internationally acclaimed annual schedule of major interdisciplinary symposia, which focus on both basic and applied frontier research fields. It has robust publishing and dissemination initiatives, works to improve science literacy, and supports the human rights of scientists. Since 2002, under the leadership of President Ellis Rubinstein, the Academy has introduced new programs to better serve its members by fostering the creation of mini-communities with shared interests. It also offers career-oriented programming for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. The Physical Sciences and Engineering program provides a critical platform for the exchange of innovative ideas and data in emerging interdisciplinary areas. In recent years, the Academy has emphasized fields such as systems biology, genome integrity, emerging infectious diseases, nanobiotechnology, cosmology, green science and sustainability, string theory, and quantitative finance. It has also developed an extensive series of electronic briefings and online multimedia postings to provide overviews of its events and those of its partners to a global scientific audience. One of the Academy's most recent initiatives is Scientists Without Borders, launched in 2006 in collaboration with the United Nations Millennium Project and other key partners. This program aims to establish a global network of scientists, institutions, academies, industry experts, and funding agencies to address critical health and other needs in the developing world. The New York Academy of Sciences was founded in 1817, originally known as the Lyceum of Natural History. Over time, it has evolved from a notable institution in the greater New York area to one of the most significant organizations in the international scientific community. Its membership has historically included prominent leaders in science, business, academia, and government, such as Presidents Thomas Jefferson and James Monroe, Alexander Graham Bell, Thomas Edison, Louis Pasteur, Charles Darwin, Margaret Mead, and Albert Einstein. By 2007, the Academy's advisory President’s Council included an unprecedented number of Nobel Laureates (23) and other luminaries from various fields. The Academy has achieved numerous historic milestones, including the publication of the first studies on environmental pollution in 1876, the first conference on antibiotics in 1946, a groundbreaking meeting on the cardiovascular effects of smoking in 1960, and the world’s first major conferences on AIDS in 1983 and SARS in 2003. It has also hosted landmark conferences addressing the unique challenges faced by women in science (1998), the intersection of music and neuroscience (2000), and the frontiers of biomedical science in China (2005). Members of the Academy played key roles in the establishment of New York University (1831) and the American Museum of Natural History (1858). In 2006, the Academy relocated to a new home on the 40th floor of 7 World Trade Center, one of the most technologically advanced green buildings in New York. This 40,000-square-foot space, equipped with state-of-the-art meeting facilities, better accommodates the needs of the Academy's growing membership and expanding programs. The Academy also presents the Heinz R. Pagels Human Rights of Scientists Award, which honors scientists who have made significant contributions to safeguarding or advancing the human rights of scientists worldwide. This award was renamed in 1986.
